text: The workshop smelled of cedar shavings and machine oil. On the bench lay a half-finished clock, its brass gears arranged in neat rows. She picked up the smallest one, turned it toward the lamp, and smiled at the tiny teeth catching the light.

Before sunrise the river held the sky like a sheet of dark glass. A heron stood at the far bank, perfectly still. Then a fish broke the surface, rings spread outward, and the bird moved at last, quick and certain, into the cold air.

The library closed at seven, but the reading room stayed warm long after. Dust drifted through the tall windows, and the shelves seemed to breathe. I found the book I wanted on the lowest shelf, tucked between two old atlases with cracked spines.

Cycling home through the hills, I learned to read the road by feel. The first climb was steady, the descent was fast, and the turn by the barn always came sooner than I expected. By the last mile my legs were tired but the sky was wide open.

Good bread begins long before the oven is warm. Flour, water, salt, and time are enough, though the dough will argue with you for hours. Fold it gently, let it rest, and trust the slow rise more than any clock on the wall.

On a clear night the old telescope showed me the rings of Saturn and four bright moons of Jupiter. I had seen the pictures a hundred times, but the real thing was different. It hung there, small and sharp, and the dark around it felt enormous.

The train left the coast at dusk and turned inland through fields of dry grass. A man across the aisle read a newspaper, folded it, and fell asleep. I watched the towns pass as points of light, each one holding lives I would never know.

In the garden, the tomatoes had taken over the path again. I tied them back with string, pulled a few weeds, and found a cucumber hidden under a broad leaf. The afternoon was hot, so I sat in the shade and listened to the bees.

The radio on the kitchen shelf only worked if you tilted it slightly to the left. Most nights it played old songs full of static, and my father hummed along while he washed the dishes. I never learned the names of those songs, but I still know the tunes.

A good map is a promise that the ground will make sense. The surveyor walks the ridge, notes every stream and fence, and writes nothing he has not seen. Months later, a stranger follows his line across the paper and finds the valley exactly where it should be.

Winter arrived without warning. One morning the pond was hard, the reeds were white, and the path had vanished under snow. We walked anyway, following the fence, and the cold made every sound sharp and close until the house appeared again.

Dear Mara, the city is louder than I remembered, but I have found a small park behind the station where the pigeons gather. I go there to write. Tell me how the orchard looks this year, and whether the old gate still sticks in the rain.
